I have listened with great interest to the hon. member for Russell, and I bow to his parliamentary experience as well as to his experience of the farming industry. I believe he made the statement that the reason for the slowness, as far as farm loan board applications were concerned,

Supply-Agriculture
is that too many lawyers have something to do with the Canadian farm loan board. That may be so. I am sure that the proposed legislation which will be brought down later this session by this government will be such that even the lawyers will be able to give some help to see that it is enacted in the proper manner and loans given without delay.
He also mentioned the fact that the small family farm in Canada needed more help, and he also referred to the health of the farmer's wife. I can go along with that. I hope perhaps he will endorse the way it is looked at down east, where it is said that in order to provide healthy farmers what you need is plenty of fresh air and buttermilk. Perhaps that is the answer. I would agree with the remarks in which he said that the family farm is important in Canada. In the constituency which I represent agriculture is quite an important industry, along with a number of others.
While I was home in the interval between the sessions I had the opportunity to attend the meeting of the Pictou-North Colchester federation of agriculture. This was the first time that I was able to attend the meetings. Along with the hon. member for Colchester-Hants and some of the members of the Nova Scotia provincial legislature I met with farmers from the area in their annual meeting. Various matters were brought up there and we were able to get a picture of farming, especially in our own area and indeed in the province of Nova Scotia. Later on the Nova Scotia federation of agriculture held a meeting in Truro which I was not able to attend, but after coming to Ottawa the executive of the Nova Scotia federation of agriculture met the Nova Scotia members and made certain recommendations and submissions. It is with a few of those submissions that I would like to deal just briefly this afternoon, Mr. Chairman. Time does not permit my going into all of them or any one of them too closely, but I believe they are important matters.
The first one is that of farm credit. During the last session I spoke in the house on the matter of farm credit, especially in reference to the province of Nova Scotia and the findings of the Hawkins commission. The Hawkins commission was set up in Nova Scotia to inquire into rural credit. Among its recommendations was something to this effect, that the provincial and federal boards, that is, the Nova Scotia land settlement board and the Canadian farm loan board, should be integrated into one and combined so as to provide more adequately for short term, intermediate and long term loans.
I was pleased to note that the Minister of Agriculture has stated that there are to

be amendments to the Canadian Farm Loan Act. I should like to thank him and also probably the Minister of Finance who will be concerned in the matter. The speech from the throne stated:
-a comprehensive review and revision of the legislation concerning farm credit, in order that credit may be more effective in assisting in the development and maintenance of an efficient and prosperous agriculture.
The amendment will be introduced at this session. As far as the province of Nova Scotia is concerned, I would say that farm credit is the crux of the whole agricultural industry and situation in that province, and that changes must be made to cover present day agricultural matters. As the legislation now stands-and as I said before in this house -it would seem that the Canadian Farm Loan Act does not cover the small farmers, and especially the farmers in the east. This is something which was pointed out by the executive of the Nova Scotia federation of agriculture in a meeting. As late as 1931 the land and buildings on a farm constituted 77 per cent of the total farm value. The submission is that today the land and buildings constitute not more than 50 per cent of the farm value and the other 50 per cent consists of stock and equipment. As we see it, so far as Nova Scotia and the maritime provinces are concerned, the act is not so constituted as to give farmers an opportunity to buy the stock and equipment necessary for modern day farming. I am glad to know that the act will be changed. I would support the government on this.
The matter of land use was also referred to by the Minister of Agriculture today. The federation of agriculture of the province of Nova Scotia pointed out to us as members that there was much good interval land in that province along the rivers which could not be taken advantage of because of the river erosion and so on. We have the Maritime Marshland Rehabilitation Act which takes care of salt water areas, and I am glad to know that a committee has been set up to study the matter of these lands in Canada and undoubtedly this matter of erosion of good land and other matters will be studied. I would recommend that after the report of this committee is brought in the government should look into this matter. Perhaps something can be done because it is a most important matter.
I should like to refer to the matter of freight rate assistance. It was pointed out by the federation, and it is recognized by the people in the Atlantic provinces, that freight rate assistance given by the government on feed grains coming from the western provinces is most important. After the recent

increase in freight rates, as shown by the further supplementary estimates which were passed in the house not too long ago, assistance was given to the eastern farmers to help them out in the matter of freight rates.
It was suggested and recommended by the hon. member for Colchester-Hants during the last session that the freight rate assistance policy should become a permanent one and should be so enacted. This is recommended by our local federation. I would suggest that the government look into this matter with a view to making it a permanent policy. It is most necessary to have this freight rate assistance because it is a great stimulus to the production of livestock in the maritime provinces. Beef cattle are now being raised in Nova Scotia. The Nova Scotia department of agriculture has set up community pastures throughout the province and an abattoir will be built in Halifax to take care of the beef and pork produce which will come to it. This was a combined effort of the government of the province of Nova Scotia and the farmers of Nova Scotia. It is being recommended and lauded a great deal because it means a lot to our cattle and hog producers. As I have said, feed grains are necessary, they are the key to the whole problem. Assistance on feed grains is most vital and I would recommend that this matter be made permanent by the government. In travelling through northern New Brunswick, particularly through the area of the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton, I was pleased to note that many of the potato producers in that area were going into beef cattle raising in order to help themselves and not be dependent on one crop only.
These are submissions which were made to the Nova Scotia members and they are most important ones. The federation of agriculture in our province is doing a good job. They are co-operating together. There are many able men in this federation and with the assistance of our able Minister of Agriculture here and with the assistance of the able minister of agriculture in the province of Nova Scotia and with the assistance of everyone, particularly the farmers in the province, the industry is going ahead and I believe will go ahead even more. It is important to our province and to many provinces, and I think we are just beginning to see the light and to put the industry really on its feet.
I do not intend to enter into discussion of the matter of wheat and deficiency payments brought up by the hon. member for Assiniboia. I will let my western colleagues say a few words on that. They probably will not be too peaceful and calm. Their words will probably make the storm outside today look 66968-9-108i

like a south sea island breeze by the time they are finished. I thought I would make a few remarks now and bring forward matters that are important to my own province.

speechtext:
That is right. Many stood up, but the great majority of the members of the house from western Canada are from one party and they have just as much right to speak as the hon. member for Assiniboia, the hon. member for Fort William or any other member. I recognize that the hon. member for Assiniboia does not want to hear what I am going to tell him now because this afternoon we heard a classic example of the extreme statements by the C.C.F. which have done more harm to agriculture in western Canada in the last 20 years than any other single thing. In his remarks he indicated that these farmers coming to Ottawa would be met with an unfriendly reception from the government side. By reading extracts from a report in the Western Producer of a speech I made, which report is entirely accurate, he left the impression that there would be an unfriendly reception. Nothing could be further from the truth.
All this started some weeks ago, Mr. Chairman, when an article appeared in a western Canada paper, the Leader-Post. There was much comment about the news story in the Leader-Post. I am going to read into the record a letter I wrote to the editor of the Star-Phoenix concerning the same subject. The letter reads as follows:
In your February 6th edition you have an editorial charging me with poor taste in doubting the grass roots character of the march on Ottawa. We have very few ways of measuring this. My personal mail for some months has run three to one asking that we stick with acreage payments. Other members report the same experience. Therefore I have to keep my mind open.

Supply-Agriculture
I would ask the privilege of pointing out the following circumstances. Your editorial appears to be based on an emasculated story that appeared in the Leader-Post. Rarely, if ever, has the Leader-Post reported a speech of mine from the series, "Report from Parliament". Yet this time it did using only selected sentences.
By contrast, the Western Producer, the organ of the wheat pool, asked for and got the full text. The farm paper may choose to disagree with me, but it will do so with all my remarks before it.
For your information, my chief concern over the march on Ottawa is not the purpose of the march but the harmful effects which may result to western agriculture. In the final paragraph of my radio address I made it clear that the federal government "will always be ready to meet and talk in good faith with western Canadian farmers at any time."
Our government will welcome the delegation because we all have a common purpose, namely, to raise the level of farm income and/or reduce farm costs. The whole matter is crystallizing into an issue of for and against immediate relief versus an attack on the fundamental problems facing agriculture. Actually we need both.
I personally am very disturbed that the tremendous pressure being put on western farmers and their organizations at the present time will make them lose sight of the basic reforms that are long overdue. Moreover, there are serious arguments against deficiency payments which are not being presented to the people.
For instance, present information is that deficiency payments, even with a $1,500 maximum, would go in large measure to larger farmers. We are trying to gather this information now, but using American estimates for their farmers the percentage is 79 per cent for 25 per cent of the farmers. I am enclosing a table showing comparative figures for two crop districts in Manitoba, one of smaller farmers and one of larger farmers. This will make clear the type of information that the western farmers should have and are not being given.
There are other points I could discuss but I will content myself with listing them.
(1)	The danger of destroying the unity of members of parliament from all parts of Canada achieved by the present government behind our national agricultural policy.
(2)	The danger of losing our oats and barley markets in the United States.
(3)	The danger of spoiling our efforts to get importing countries to reduce wheat subsidies.
(4)	The danger of getting into the same financial difficulties as the United States which resulted from their use of a fixed parity price concept instead of striving for a parity of income.
(5)	The danger of disrupting the present shift towards greater diversification of farm production.
I trust that these thoughts will add something to the present debate.
The Star-Phoenix took that letter, printed it and included the table that I gave them, and by so doing rendered a great service to the farmers of that area of western Canada.
There is another thing that happened in the debate. I came into the house toward the last part of the speech of the hon. member for Assiniboia. He was making certain statements and was reading from a story in the Western Producer which was an exact replica of my speech. I asked him the question: Do you deny that the Liberals and the
[Mr. Hamilton (Qu'Appelle) .3
C.C.F. cuddled up in 1946 in support of the British wheat agreement? The British wheat agreement was opposed by only one party in Canada, the Progressive Conservative party led by John Bracken who warned that certain things would happen if the government went through with this madness. That agreement did not come from the grass roots at all but was imposed from the top by a group of people led, I believe, by the then minister of agriculture, the then minister of trade and commerce and certain farm leaders who went back and told western farmers that they must support the agreement to guarantee high prices after the agreement was ended.
If any person wants to read about this, go back to the debates in Hansard for August, 1946. Read the remarks of Walter Tucker, the ex-member for Rosthern. Read the remarks of the leader of the Progressive Conservative party in those days, John Bracken. There you will find one of the greatest sell-outs of the western farmer that you ever saw. Nor was this the end of it. These same gentlemen came back to western Canada and joined in the attack on the Conservative party in the election of 1949. Because we were pointing out all the facts and dangers of the British wheat agreement to western Canadian farmers they accused us of being friends of the grain exchange. In fact, the C.C.F. did such a wonderful job of scaring the people silly in western Canada with respect to what we stood for, the right of the farmer to decide his own future instead of it being decided by government leaders at Ottawa, that there was hardly a C.C.F. member elected in the 1949 campaign. In 1945 the majority of members from Saskatchewan were C.C.F., but in 1949 they almost disappeared and the Liberals took over because they had scared the voters so badly the voters felt they had to turn to the only party that could stop the Conservatives.
This British wheat agreement cost the western farmers, by best estimates, about $600 million and I know how desperately the farmers would like to have some of that $600 million today. The most amazing thing is that farm organizations at the rank and file level, and political parties at the rank and file level, have been through a very rough time in Saskatchewan in the last 25 years. This applies to our prairie provinces generally. About three years ago it seemed that peace was coming because the members of every political party, Social Credit, Liberal, C.C.F., Conservative and every other party of which I have heard out there, were all saying pretty well the same thing about what the agricultural industry required. The farm organizations got together and, for the first

time, we had a unanimity of opinion in 1956 that has never existed since because of this ramp on deficiency payments.
Deficiency payments are a proper thing to discuss. There are certain arguments for them and certain arguments against them. However, when all the arguments and all the propaganda are in favour of one side, then somebody has to have the courage to stand up and put forth the facts concerning the other side. There are people who believe differently. The hon. member for Assiniboia mentioned his own bill of rights. I have said in this house that I could support every point in the bill of rights he enunciated in his speech at Crane Valley, Saskatchewan. This is the type of speech that western Canada needs, and the type of speech that agriculture in western Canada needs. Agriculture does not need the type of generalization and conflicting statements which were made today because all they do is rend and divide.
The Winnipeg Tribune of January 24 carried a newspaper story concerning the program of the Manitoba federation of agriculture. I have a copy here, and there are some six immediate points and 12 long range points. Not once in this series of 18 points mentioned is there any mention of deficiency payments. I could support almost everything in this program now. I could have supported it last year and I could next year. This is a sound, constructive report as to what they think agriculture needs. I know the hon. member for Assiniboia knows what should be done and I know the members of the Manitoba federation of agriculture know what should be done. However, when they, as farm leaders, are faced with the tremendous pressure of television shows two or three times a week, radio programs and an army of 7,000 people out collecting names on petitions, it is very difficult for a moderate, responsible farm leader to stand up in front of what looks like an avalanche. But somebody does have to stand up occasionally and speak his mind about what he believes is true. This is what I attempted to do in that speech of February 4 or 5, whatever the date was. I did not make the speech in any attempt at being derogatory to the march. I simply said, and other people were noticing the same thing, that this appeared to be a great promotion from above and I am always suspicious of anything that is promoted from above. I point that out, that these farm leaders from all across the west come and tell us that this federation program is what they want.
I am not finished with this thing yet. One of the great things that we have accomplished as a government is that we have brought
Supply-Agriculture
members of parliament from all parts of Canada to recognize that this agricultural problem is not only in western Canada, it is in every part of Canada. The hon. member for Russell was speaking today about his constituency. The same speech could be made for many ridings across this country. This is a national problem. Any effort made to try to pit the west against the east or the maritimes against Ontario or anything else like that is an effort to destroy the work of people who desperately need constructive help. I am going to read to you two paragraphs from an address delivered by Mr. Wesson on November 10, 1958.
I quote:
Even in the election campaign between January and March, questions were put to speakers in the country and they always gave the same answer- the government is continuing to give careful consideration to this whole question. And it was not until the end of August that we got an official denial and something else proposed in its place, after the rejection of the principle of deficiency payments as proposed by the three wheat pools.
He is referring to the Prime Minister's statement in the house in August laying down the seven points for a national agricultural policy.
Then, he goes on and says to these delegates:
I am not going to tell you what you should do before this discussion is closed, but in view of what happened with government policy, it is obvious to me with conversations that we had with private members from western Canada as well as ministers, that eastern Canada had a good deal to do with this final decision on this paltry $40 million and that is the reason why eastern Canada has got to get some education.
Now, this country, so long divided on many issues, so long divided by regional problems, has been able to get a government, under the banner of a great Canadian, to collect the people from all parts of this country, from all walks of life, and get them to see that there was a national problem in agriculture. This party supported that national agricultural policy in this house 100 per cent. This was unity of a real sort, and yet here we have this effort to divide.
This problem of agriculture cannot be resolved by pitting the west against the east and it was for that reason I charged, in my opening remarks, that the type of speech delivered here by the hon. member for Assiniboia was another classic example of the type of thing that stirs the emotions and divides the country on basic economic issues.

In achieving these goals-

Then it goes on and lists 10 points in that basic approach. This same theme is carried out in all the volumes. If any person wants to know where this government is going, one of the best ways to find out is to go through these 14 volumes and read their conclusions and recommendations. We look at these volumes and they play a great part in our final decisions. We also look at many other sources of information because we are seriously trying to make up for almost a quarter of a century of inactivity on the agricultural front by the previous government. Liberals today in my province know that their party would not be where it is if they had moved to grapple with these extremely complex and difficult problems. No reasonable farmer expects any government to come up with final answers in one, two or three years. All he expects from his government is an honest and intelligent effort. As long as we have in this house, not only men like the Prime Minister but like the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Trade and Commerce, doing the type of work they are doing there is no question in my mind as to how these same farmers who supported us in 1957 and to a greater degree in 1958 will stand at the next appeal to the people.

But we at least feel, particularly with our stabilization bill in effect and beginning to take hold, that the long fight upwards for better prices and a better return

to the farmer is beginning to show results. I mention that matter with some feeling because I know that I must be honest with my own farm constituents. I know that any politician who says to them, "Vote for me and I will cure all your problems with some price change" is just fooling those people. That is the type of thing that I said in the election campaigns of 1953, 1957 and 1958 and I hope I can say it again when the next election comes.

That was the stand that I took.
I put it this way. I would not support any policy where a greater proportion of the money went to the larger farmers and a smaller proportion went to the more numerous small farmers. I do not back down from that stand. But if anybody can show me how deficiency payments will help the little farmer lift himself up and get out of this situation where his gross income is so low, then I am always willing to listen. But I look at the figures showing the amount of wheat, oats and barley sold by a small farmer in my riding and

I see the difference all through the north eastern part of Saskatchewan and through Manitoba. I do not care if you raise the price to $3 a bushel, you could not lift up the level of living of some of the farmers in my riding. They must feed their oats, their barley and some of their wheat to stock in order to make any sort of income at all. Yet this thing is designed to force them to sell to the elevator in order to get the deficiency payment. I could go on and discuss this matter at greater length but I think I have said enough to make my own stand clear.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I want to remind the committee that last August when the Prime Minister stood up here and outlined that statement on the national agricultural policy it was a great day in Canada's history as far as the farmer was concerned. How many times have you heard the hon. member for Assiniboia discuss this farm program enunciated by the Prime Minister and taking a look at all its aspects, how it is trying to get at this question of the sale of our products; how it is trying to stabilize prices by a forward pricing system; how it is trying to stabilize the effect of weather calamities by crop insurance; how it is trying to give to the young farmer and the small farmer and even help the older farmer to sell his land; some help in doing the things that will make his farm operation more efficient and give a chance to see what we in the Conservative party stand for, namely the family farm all across Canada.
I wonder if the hon. member for Assiniboia has considered the great need for constructive suggestions on a rural development program? I know we are working on it, but I would like the views of the hon. members of this house, and I know the Minister of Agriculture would. I would like to hear various suggestions in connection with this program to help the smaller farmer, or any farmer, meet the technological problems which have arisen, as well as the problems of the machine age. I could discuss other things, such as research and so on, but I would like to put it in this way. If any hon. member would sit down and make a list of these various steps, which are only the seven main steps of a huge program, and figure out the amount of money that the people of Canada would be willing to put behind a constructive, comprehensive farm program, then the danger of threatening that great program by trying to divert farm organization attention away from the need of a comprehensive program to an isolated act will be realized.

Mr. Chairman, up to the present the committee has heard the voices of experts on the subject of agriculture. Now

Supply-A griculture
for a few moments I beg your indulgence to listen to a few remarks from an amateur. I want to assure hon. members that I will not speak until the deadline, so that all of us will be able to say a few words.
The district in which the two fine cities of Fort William and Port Arthur are located is not a prosperous agricultural area comparable to the prairie provinces, or even to the eastern portion of Ontario. But in the rugged terrain of Thunder bay there are numerous dairy and truck garden farms. They are small, with a few exceptions. We have, however, large tracts of empty barren area that could be profitably put to farming use if the prospective farmer had the means of acquiring machinery and stocks. The majority of those small farmers who are now engaged in farming in my constituency need assistance in the form of loans. At the present time unless a farmer has collateral assets it is virtually impossible for him to obtain a loan from a bank, and even the farm loan board is not always sympathetic to his need. I believe that the hon. member for Cape Breton South had the same thing in mind when he spoke a few moments ago about the needs of the farmers in Nova Scotia. I am very much concerned with the small farmer who is operating a comparatively small piece of land, judged by western farm standards, and who is making his living wholly from his produce.
Another important aspect of the small farm which should be considered is that a farm is a good place to bring up a large family. A lot of people are entering Canada through immigration channels, so let us start a number of small farms where there is plenty of room and fresh air, which is an ideal environment in which to raise children, whose worth to Canada transcends any consideration of small assistance in the way of a loan. I realize that this is a problem which concerns the provinces as much as the federal government. However, when we visualize the national benefit that would be derived from the over-all growth and prosperity of Canada by giving active encouragement to these people we should consider immediate steps to devise ways and means to assist those who are ready and willing to go on the land. It seems to me that while the government is very much interested in the wheat farming of the west and the fruit and tobacco farms of the east, it does not show the same zeal for the welfare of the small farmer of northwestern Ontario.
I am in full accord with the proposal to establish an independent research organization as suggested by the interprovincial farm union council, with representation from the

district of Thunder bay. We have qualified farmers in our district who could make a substantial contribution to such a research council. In any such organization a capable representative from northwestern Ontario should be essential, because farming in that part of the province of Ontario raises problems which are not prevalent in other parts of Canada. If a research council is to be established, such council should be made operative for all types of farming and not be only of benefit to the wheat farmers. It should also embrace the problem of the small mixed farmers, whose facilities for the development of their holdings are very limited. These are types of farms involving practices which do not apply to other areas; hence the importance of expert advice and assistance, beginning with the establishment of a policy which would enable the small farmers to obtain long term loans from the farm loan board, which at present, as I have indicated, because of undue restrictions does not meet the exigencies and requirements of the average farmer of northwestern Ontario.
In closing, I am going to ask the minister to indicate if the government is considering the establishment of a research council and, secondly, has the government any land loan policy which would be of benefit to small farmers?

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in rising to take part in this debate I would like to be permitted to express my appreciation for some of the proposed legislation for this session pertaining to agriculture. As a western farmer it was very gratifying to me to hear that a national crop insurance plan will be presented to th ehouse for its consideration. This long sought legislation asked for by farmers and authorities on agriculture for many years is a very important and essential legislation and is long overdue. When I think back over the years when acres and acres of farm land in the west were flooded and could never be sown to crops; or when I think back to the years when land that was sown could never be harvested because of heavy fall rain and the crop had to be left in the fields over the winter to deteriorate to the point where it never could be harvested; or when I think of beautiful stands of grain wiped out, together with the farmers' hopes, by one hour's frost; then and only then can one understand what a national crop insurance scheme could mean to a farmer. Our Prime Minister is familiar with these hazards, and on August 30 last he spoke in the house about his intention to introduce legislation dealing with crop insurance.

The other legislation awaiting parliamentary approval concerns improved conditions of farm credit. We have heard much about the need of young farmers to establish themselves on economic farm units, but it would be both useless and senseless for us to keep talking about this if we cannot provide them with the necessary means of making their farms economic units either by diversifying them, enlarging them or by using the latest farm methods and equipment. All this can only be done if long term credit is made available to enable all these things to be accomplished. Many of our younger farmers, who wanted to make farming their life occupation have been handicapped because they could not qualify for farm loan credits.
But the most welcome and heart warming words which I have heard for a long time were those which spelled out this government's recommendation to review the discriminatory effects of horizontal freight rates and the latest increases. What do these increased freight rates mean to the farmer in the west and in the maritimes, and how do they affect their economies?
To give hon. members a true picture, and illustrate my point, I must take the committee back to the year 1947. If a farmer bought a harvester combine in that year he had to have it shipped to his home town in the west, and was charged $300 for freight. Ten years later, in 1957, let us suppose he has to replace his combine. Suppose he buys the same kind of machine, a machine of the same size which suits his farm best. Again he has to ship the combine to his farm, but this time the freight bill is not $300, it is a figure twice as high. Why is this? It is because freight rates had been allowed to increase by 125 per cent during the 10-year period. But this is not the end of the story. The manufacturer, too, had to pay a higher freight rate on the materials used to build this combine-125 per cent more in 1957 than in 1947. Of course, as far as the manufacturer was concerned this only meant that he had to increase the price of the combine by the amount of the additional freight it cost him.
The simple truth illustrated by this example of the purchase of a combine is that in freight rates alone the price rose during that 10-year period by between 200 and 300 per cent. However, a harvester is not the only piece of machinery which a farmer has to buy. He needs many more implements such as tractors, drills, and so on, the list seeming to be unending once a farmer begins to buy machinery. And farmers must pay freight on them all, whether they 66968-9-109
Supply-Agriculture
buy an $8,000 combine or whether they sell and ship their own products. For them it is a one way street, coming and going. Mr. Chairman, are you still wondering why the cost of farm production is so high, and what the facts are behind the price squeeze?
Freight rates are one most important factor about which we have heard many complaints. These discriminatory freight rates should never have been allowed to come into force. The Turgeon royal commission recommended that horizontal freight rate increases were unfair and unjust. Nevertheless they were allowed to go on year after year until they reached the point where they were a staggering 125 per cent above the 1947 level. Our party, in opposition at that time, sounded a warning and pointed out the serious consequences these increases would have on our economy, but nothing was done. Of course, we are not washing our hands as if to say it is not our fault and nothing can be done to remedy the situation. This government has recognized that a serious problem exists, and has undertaken to revise the whole freight rate structure so as to avoid the detrimental effects of a horizontal freight rate increase.
Speaking of freight rates, I should like to bring to the attention of the committee another unjust freight rate, namely the freight rate on rapeseed. The present freight rate structure will definitely restrict the development of the rapeseed industry. In order that hon. members may be able to compare the figures, may I say that the freight rate on wheat, oats, barley and rye from Saskatoon to Fort William is 22 cents per hundredweight: the rate for flax is 23| cents per hundredweight. The rate for rapeseed, however, is no less than 70 cents per hundredweight. Cereal grains and flax are covered by the Crownest pass agreement, but rapeseed is not. Consequently, rapeseed is subjected to further increases in freight rates as they become effective. At the present time, the railways have a further application pending for a 17 per cent increase in freight rates. Applied to rapeseed this would bring the rate from Saskatoon to Fort William to 82 cents per hundredweight. Unless action is taken to modify the effect of present rates, production will be curtailed and acreage now growing rapeseed will again be put under wheat.
Rapeseed cannot be competitive in the situation I have described. The handling, marketing and storage of rapeseed are processes identical with those carried out in the case of other grains. Rapeseed is accepted and carried by ocean carriers at the same rate as flax or other grains to all parts of the world and lake freighters carry rapeseed at the same rate as they carry other grains.

Seemingly the only people who do not recognize rapeseed as a grain are the Canadian railways. Yet the railroads incur no more costs in handling rapeseed than are incurred in handling any other grain; there is no difference between rapeseed and flax when it comes to transportation.
In addition to freight rates, tariffs have also affected the expansion of this branch of the industry. Rapeseed, when processed, is manufactured into an edible oil comparable to soybean oil, or any of the other oils on the vegetable oil market.
Progress reported.

maintopic: BOILER INSPECTION AND INSURANCE COMPANY OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, clause 3 of the bill as it appears reads this way:
The three thousand shares of the company issued and outstanding prior to the passing of this act and having a par value of one hundred dollars each shall be subdivided into thirty thousand of the aforesaid shares having a par value of ten dollars each on the basis of ten shares for one. The said thirty thousand ordinary shares shall constitute the total issued capital of the company at the date of the coming into force of this act.
At the time this bill was being dealt with by the banking and commerce committee some question was raised to the language used in

this clause, although there was no difference of opinion, or no disapproval of what was being sought to be done by the clause, or what the petitioners were asking to be done. Following that discussion and because I had taken a rather active part in it in committee, I took the opportunity of consulting with the law clerks on the question of the draftsmanship of the clause and I found that some of the views I held on the draftsmanship were supported, and some additional points of view were expressed on them. I got a rather lengthy opinion from the parliamentary counsel and the assistant law clerk. I think it is not necessary to take up the time of the committee on the points raised but perhaps I should say a word or two about them. It will be noted that in the third line-that is, line 30 of the bill now before the committee-the words "shall be subdivided" are used. The provision is that the existing shares of the compnay now in existence shall be subdivided when the new legislation now before us comes into effect. Then, in the last sentence this statement is made:
The said thirty thousand ordinary shares shall constitute the total issued capital of the company at the date of the coming into force of this act.
That is, presumably, the new shares. It was pointed out that probably the difficulty in language can be corrected by simply striking out the words "shall be" in line 30 and substituting therefor the word "are". But there are still further difficulties in the language because, referring to the point of time and the coming into force of the act the expression is used in the second and third lines, "prior to the passing of this act" and then, in referring to the point of time at the very end of the clause, the expression is used, "at the date of the coming into force of this act." It will be seen that there is a looseness of terminology there. It will be further seen that in line 33 of the clause the words, "the said thirty thousand shares" appear, when there are no said thirty thousand shares. It seems to me that the use of these words is not accurate and it is capable of a good deal of confusion. The result of it all is that I think there should be new language and the suggested language which I propose to move after I have read it is the language suggested by the parliamentary counsel and the assistant law clerk, which reads:
Each of the 3,000 shares of the company issued and outstanding and having a par value of $100 is hereby subdivided into 10 shares having a par value of $10 each, so that the capital stock of the company now issued and outstanding shall consist of 30,000 shares having a total par value of $300,000.

That is the clause suggested by the officials. Therefore I should like to move, seconded by the hon. member for Colchester-Hants (Mr. Kennedy):
That clause 3 of Bill S-8, an act respecting the Boiler Inspection and Insurance Company of Canada, be deleted, and that the following be substituted therefor:
"Each of the 3,000 shares of the company issued and outstanding and having a par value of $100 is hereby subdivided into 10 shares having a par value of $10 each, so that the capital stock of the company now issued and outstanding shall consist of 30,000 shares having a total par value of $300,000."

speakeroldname: Mr. D. M. Fisher (Port Arthur) moved
subtopic: EXTENSION OF RIGHT TO VOTE AT ADVANCE POLLS
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-10, to amend the Canada Elections Act (voting at advance polls).
He said: The disconcerting speed with which we have moved in processing bills today is in marked contrast to the fate of this particular bill, because this is the fifth time it has been introduced into the house and each time it has been garlanded with all sorts of approval. Everyone seems to think there is a marvelous principle involved in this particular bill, but it is usually talked out. Fortunately today the time during which it can be talked out is not going to be very long. I am pleased to see the minister who is responsible for this particular department in attendance. I am pleased also to see the tall member for Halifax, the hon. member for York-Scarborough (Mr. McGee) and the other member from Toronto, whom we usually see when bills are to be talked out. I hope they will pass around the honours today.
The Canada Elections Act is peculiarly an act that is handled within the House of Commons framework. The executive takes much less of a lead in regard to amendments to this act. This act is much more sensitive to the opinion of hon. members. It is traditional that during the first session after an election when most grievances with regard to the act are sharper the standing

Canada Elections Act
committee on privileges and elections does not sit. The sittings of this committee are postponed until the second session. I have a good hunch when the next election is going to be. It is going to be sometime in late May or early June of 1962. The reason it is going to be then is, of course, that with the great majority the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) has he can call an election at any time. It will not be any later than that because if it is later he will have to go to the people with a completely new distribution of seats which will mean the losing of at least three seats in Saskatchewan. The Prime Minister comes from there and I am assuming he will not want to fight the next election on that basis, so I have deduced the date to be early June, 1962.
This does give us some considerable time to make changes in the Canada Elections Act. I think there is almost universal agreement, even amongst such generally contradictory bodies as the Canadian chamber of commerce and the Canadian Labour Congress, that we need to extend the advance polling privileges. This privilege is limited now to a few occupations. The general reason for extending the scope has to do with changes in society. We have much more mobility in our labour force; many more sales personnel on the road and wider distances to cover. People are planning their vacations to a greater extent, even planning them months ahead because it is possible to make that type of arrangement now which cannot be altered even for such a fundamental as casting a vote.
The principle involved in this particular bill is a very simple one. The amendment seeks to extend the privilege of voting at advance polls to any Canadian who is aware of the fact he is not going to be at his proper polling place on election day. This is really all the bill does, and that is the principle involved. It has been noticeable in previous debates that speakers who approved of the principle and wanted to have enough time to talk the bill out always dove into the actual provisions of the bill.
Hon. members have been critical of several points, and one of those points has been the feeling that the regulation involved in this particular bill will make it difficult in rural polls. I should like to put it to most hon. members, not so much in contradiction of that but in balance, that the people in rural polls have a tremendous advantage in so far as voting is concerned over the people in urban polls. Provided a voter in a rural poll can get a neighbour to identify him, he can be sworn in and cast his vote. However,

this provision does not apply to urban polls and it is in urban polls where the greatest pressure exists for advance polling privileges, not only because they are the more populous but because they are the polls in which there are more people who are moving in society.
The hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) has another bill on the order paper relating to absentee voting. This is something with which the standing committee on privileges and elections will have to deal. I should like to remind hon. members that there is a distinction between the two. I have to say, fairly and truthfully, that what we need is a complete revision of the Canada Elections Act from a fairly wide point of view. A thorough study is needed to assess the merits of the various schemes of absentee voting and voting at advance polls. The absentee voting system is really designed so that no matter where you are in Canada you can vote for a particular candidate in your particular constituency. This is not such an urgent problem as voting at advance polls, that is in the sense of a real grievance, but it also needs to be considered.
We have some marvelous examples in British Columbia, Saskatchewan, and to a degree in Ontario and Manitoba, where very serious and sincere efforts have been made to extend this particular privilege to more people. I think, in the main, they have worked well. Last year I touched on one of the weaknesses of the extension of advance polling privileges in Ontario, and that was the relatively high cost in relation to the number of votes cast. However, we are going to have an election in Ontario this year. It seems to be in the cards, and I think we will find that the advance polling privilege will be used much more this time than it was last, when the people, especially the party organizations, were not so aware of it.
Now, the final point I wanted to make in so far as the bill is concerned is that the principle is a good one. I think almost everyone will recognize that there is hardly a member of parliament who has not been haunted at election time, and especially on election day, by phone calls from people who have not been able to vote because of the narrowness of the restriction of this privilege. There really is no reason why a commercial traveller or a transport worker should have an advantage in voting over someone who, because of the nature of his employment, is forced to be away on election day.
This particular lack disenfranchised hundreds of voters in my own constituency in the last election. They are woods workers and were covered and put on a poll list out

in the woods camp. It just so happened that between the time they were registered as voters and polling day these camps were closed down and the majority of the men moved into urban polls where they could not be sworn in. Hence that whole group was disenfranchised. I am not saying that this particular legislation would cure that particular difficulty but it would tend to cure it in that it would give them a longer period in which to vote. I hope it would fit in with the other changes in the election act that would give them a chance to vote such as extending to the urban polls the privilege that people now have in the rural polls.
The electoral officer this particular house has to deal with is a well-informed gentleman. He has helped to a degree in conection with almost all the bills that private members have brought in with respect to changing the Canada Elections Act. At the very least he has provided a tremendous amount of information. I hope the present minister who has the responsibility and the present chairman of the standing committee on privileges and elections are in close touch with the chief electoral officer. I know the spirit and the general attitude of the chief electoral officer and his senior officials is a progressive one; I mean it is progressive in the sense that they are as much aware as we are or perhaps more so, of the tedious administrative difficulties involved in changes in the act but also in bringing the privilege of voting and the right of voting to more people. For that reason I should like to see someone move that this bill, after the principle has been approved, be referred to the standing committee on privileges and elections.
After this particular committee has heard from the electoral officer and from the various members who have an interest in this kind of amendment and change, this particular bill could be the focal point for considering that particular aspect of the Canada Elections Act. I think it would provide the members of the committee with a starting point that would be a good relative consideration in relation to the present regulations. Certainly I believe the difficulties involved in the consequential changes arising out of this bill are going to be encountered in making adjustments. I think this particular bill and the bill on absentee voting would be an excellent starting point for major changes in the elections act with regard to polling.
Despite what I seem to feel is a thickening lethargy and a thickening disinterest on the part of many government members on such matters, I feel that this particular change is going to come before the election in late May or June of 1962.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF RIGHT TO VOTE AT ADVANCE POLLS
speechtext:
I beg your pardon, Mr. Speaker; but it was an opportunity to reply to the consistent and persistent interruptions from that section of the house.
As far as my views are concerned on this particular bill, I approve the principle of it with reservations. My reasons for approving the principle apply in particular to some of the aspects of the bill mentioned by the hon. member for Port Arthur. I would refer to such people as holidayers, employees of companies, of which there are large numbers in my riding-and I used to be one myself-who have virtually no choice when they will take their holidays. They apply early in the year, months and months

Canada Elections Act
ahead, to take their holidays at a particular week or period of one or two weeks in the summer, late spring or early fall. When an election is called after that decision is made these people have no opportunity to alter that holiday period and they are either at the cottage or resort some hundreds of miles away from their normal place of residence, or are touring through the many beauty spots of Canada or the United States. I think it is asking a great deal to ask a person, particularly one such as I was in recent years, with two short weeks to enjoy in a regular working year, to leave a cottage two or three hundred miles away, spend the better part of two or three days in getting back home and then to drive back to the cottage or to interrupt touring plans in order to return home to vote.
I approve the principle as it applies and as this bill will obviously assist such persons. The same thing applies to employees of commercial firms in capacities other than those covered by the present act. While a travelling salesman operating on commission certainly is entitled to go to the advance poll under the present regulations, a man working for someone else again has no choice. He is told to go to a certain place at a certain time. While we have many responsible employers in this country who try to avoid the possibility of this difficulty costing a man his vote, unfortunately there are many who either do not consider it in time or who have plans which have been made so far in advance that it is impossible to change them.
These are the obvious reasons and there are many others. I have been looking over the debates on this bill in the past two sessions. What I should like to discuss for a few moments are some of the problems inherent in the holding of an earlier poll. I suggest there are serious difficulties in this matter and prodigious problems as far as I myself am concerned.
One aspect of that argument, of course, is that an election is something like a jury trial. The electors are the jury and the candidates present their cases to that jury. It seems to me that at a period of something like ten days before an election all the evidence is simply not in. Issues are developing and move from side to side. Public opinion sways back and forth between the two major candidates. It raises doubts in my mind from what I have seen of municipal, provincial and federal elections. You have to contend with the well known technique of the smear campaign. A statement is made late enough in the election that it is impossible for the person who is alleged to

have committed an offence to have the opportunity to reply to it. How this would affect the results of an advance poll raises serious questions in my mind.
Another thing I am concerned about is, what percentage of the voters eligible to vote in advance polls will vote? I know from reading previous debates that reference was made by the then member for Winnipeg North Centre to recent elections in Manitoba. I think he described the percentage of advance poll voters as relatively small. I think the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Morton) last year made reference to the fact that in the Ontario election in 1955 again the numbers were small. I would like to know what sort of percentages we are dealing with here. What are the anticipated percentages in the event that the scope of this particular aspect of the act is widened? It seems to me, on examining the records of elections over the years, that the percentage difference between the votes of the two major parties which decide who shall form the government, and the percentages in individual cases of candidates in most of the federal elections in our history, has been relatively small. I am wondering if there is a danger, when you are increasing the percentage of those who make the decision at a time when, as I have suggested, the evidence is not in and the picture is not complete, that this might have quite a serious result. Certainly in a close election it could have a decisive effect on the result. The percentage increases, as I think it will when people become accustomed to these new voting habits. Is this likely to result in two campaigns in one? Is it likely to result in a campaign designed to appeal to that section of the electorate which would be voting earlier and then a later campaign designed to focus upon the final election date?
I mentioned earlier that this would pose a virtually insurmountable problem in my own case. There are in my constituency at the moment about a quarter of a million people. My estimate is that by the time the next election rolls around there will be approximately a third of a million. As to what the number of voters might be is very difficult to assess. There are large numbers of young children in my riding, and many young families. However, the simple problem does remain, that in my case I can inform the electorate what my name is, what my party is, and so on, in the form of a postcard to them, but if this legislation is enacted, how can I tell these people the simple facts without going broke in the process? My estimate is that it would cost me something like

$3,000 to pay for the stamps to put on the postcards to tell the electors in my riding who I am.
If there is going to be an appreciable number of the electors in my riding voting at an advance poll, the question arises, should I send this information out ten or even fifteen days before the election? Obviously if there are going to be an appreciable number of persons voting I am in trouble, because I must contact them either too early or wait until later in the election and I cannot do both. I was hoping I would have heard some discussion from the hon. member who introduced this bill as to the numbers he has in mind when he suggests that these advance polls be moved back as the bill indicates. If any other member speaking to this bill has any ideas on this subject, I would be most interested to hear them. As I said at the beginning, Mr. Speaker, I favour the principle of this bill, but I have some reservations about its application in my particular case in the next election.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was happy to hear the member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) clarify two things this afternoon. He told us first when the next federal election will be, and he has told us when the next Ontario provincial election will likely be. I am sure now that we know these facts we can prepare ourselves accordingly.
In rising to speak to this question, I, like the other two members, agree with the principle. I think all of us who have taken part in elections, even before we had our nominations-when perhaps we were working for others who were federal candidates- appreciate the fact that in many cases people who are entitled to vote and have the qualifications under the act were denied the right to vote because they were absent. In principle I go along with the terms and conditions of the amendment in question. The explanatory notes very simply put states:
The privilege of voting at an advance poll is now restricted to a limited number of voters, namely commercial travellers, fishermen, persons employed upon railways, vessels, airships, etc., members of the reserve forces, the R.C.M.P. etc.
It does seem, on examining and discussing this matter with the people who feel they have the privilege of voting in their absence, that because they do not fill in their application they are denied their franchise. On examining the bill itself one is faced with two or three questions. I want to deal with some of the questions which might affect a rural constituency, particularly one like mine, Bow River, in Alberta. In rural constituencies it would seem, when setting up advance polls, that it would be necessary
Canada Elections Act
that all communities, all villages or towns, have an advance poll. In that instance there would be an increase in the number of advance polls. The way the position stands at the moment, I only have a very small portion of the city of Calgary along by the Bow river and thgre is only one advance poll. Under the amendment, if it passed, it would mean we would have to have advance polls in all the towns and villages in some of the rural communities, because if the act is to be equitable and carry out in principle what it intends, then it would be very unfair for a man in one constituency to travel 35 miles while another man travels only one mile. There would have to be a lot more advance polls, and when we run into that sort of thing it would affect the question of the cost of running an election.
There is a second point I should like to make. I am sure it is one which has been considered by others in the past because I understand this bill has been before the house on previous occasions. The time between the date of nomination and the date of the election would be extended under the terms of the act by at least one week, which would make it three weeks instead of two. The reason for that is that because of the number of advance polls which would take place in these circumstances it would be necessary for the deputy returning officer to tally the number of advance votes so that there would be no duplication. Then you would have to set up special machinery for advance polls similar to the machinery set up in the ordinary poll on voting day, complete with clerks, scrutineers and other officials-almost a duplication. This would, of course, work some hardship on the candidates themselves because they would have to have agents working for three or four days instead of on the one day at the election as presently required and that, of course, would result in extra expense.
It would be necessary for a candidate to have such scrutineers or agents, because if arrangements are not made similar to those made at the polls on election day there is always the chance of something taking place which is not quite according to law. This may seem like a digression, but it might be helpful to give an example of what happened at one of the polls when I first became a candidate in the election of 1957. I attended one of the polls and I saw two or three people handing out literature. This happened to be a facsimile of the ballot, on the back of which was a picture of my main opponent and the words: on the other side, see how to mark your ballot. And the people were able to take the ballot handed out-the facsimile-into the voting booth and mark the

Canada Elections Act ballot accordingly. That is the reason why we have provision for scrutineers in the original act, and that is why we should have to have candidates' agents present all the time. That is why it is clearly set out in the act that the principle of equity for all shall apply. If matters were left entirely to the discretion of the returning officers there would be a different system in every poll and in every constituency across the country and there would be no uniformity at all.
I have not done a great deal of research on this, but it does seem to me that some of the suggestions which were made by the hon. member for Port Arthur had merit and that they could profitably be studied in committee. With regard to the idea of an absentee voting system, I do know from my experience as a practising lawyer that Americans have come into my office in order to have certain documents notarized, thus entitling them to vote in elections at home. I believe this system is also used in certain countries of the commonwealth. It should be compared, in my opinion, with the system of advance polls which would be more costly and more cumbersome because it would mean a three-day election set up instead of the one-day system we have at present.
In summary I should like to repeat the main points I have raised. If this amendment were to carry it would mean the setting up of a number of advance polls. Second, there would have to be a greater time between the date of the nomination and the election date in order that the returning officer could get in all the returns so that it could be ascertained that those who had taken advantage of the advance poll in question had been removed from the voters list. Third, there would have to be special machinery set up which, again, would be more costly. Last, but not least it would impose something of a burden on candidates themselves, because they would be running a three-day election instead of a one-day election.
Before I sit down I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Port Arthur for presenting this amendment to the present act. As I understand it, the Canada Elections Act has not been changed for a number of years. The amendment deals with one of the major problems which all candidates encounter in an election. There are numbers of people who are denied their right to the franchise, and I feel that in a democracy if a man is absent because of business reasons or for some reason beyond his control he should not be prevented from voting. The hon. member for Port Arthur made a good point when he differentiated between the type of rules and 

regulations governing city polls and those governing rural polls. In the rural poll it is always possible for an applicant to be sworn in, but a person in a city poll is denied this privilege. Unless he checks the voters list and finds his name there or takes action in the period which is set before the election, he cannot take part.
I think we should streamline the act somewhat and make it possible for every qualified person in Canada to have the privilege of exercising his vote, whether he is at home on the day of the election or not. This legislation is equitable in its effect upon all, whether we support the Liberal party, the C.C.F. party or the Conservative party. We all know that it is a free contest in this democracy of ours, and we want to see such rules and regulations set up under the election act as will be fair to one and all.

I see it is nearly six o'clock, Mr. Speaker. I had quite a number of points I wished to add to this debate. Perhaps I might point out, however, that schedule 2 of the election act does provide for the constitution of advance polls across the country. At the present time there are approximately 150 towns, cities and villages which are able to hold advance polls. I have been advised by the chief electoral officer that in the last election about 250 advance polls were actually in existence because of the fact that some of the larger cities often had one advance poll per constituency. One advance poll was held in my own riding, and I know it was a busy poll.
Unfortunately, too few of our citizens have the privilege of voting at advance polls. There are many people such as loggers, miners, prospectors, and so on who, because of the rigid requirements of our election act, are in effect disenfranchised.
